summary:
We built Blink, a web app that turns real data from NASA's SPHEREx infrared space telescope into a time-lapse and starlight explorer anyone can use. Because SPHEREx captures near-infrared light (0.75 to 5.0 µm) that is completely invisible to the human eye, we translated those 102 hidden wavelengths into false-color images and animations so anyone can interact with what the telescope detects.

In the past astronomers would dig through raw telescope files, "Blinking" mechanically with glass photo plates (which is how Pluto was discovered)! now with Blink you can type in coordinates and flip between SPHEREx data, plus older 2010 WISE and 2014 to 2024 NEOWISE photos. Watching those images play in sequence lets you see nearby stars and brown dwarfs move across a 16-year timeline. 

With public data provided by NASA, you can flip between dates, subtract older photos from newer ones to isolate what changed, build custom false-color images from 102 infrared wavelengths, and click any star to see its brightness over time.  You can also download science-ready data files, save looping GIFs of moving stars, and listen to starlight patterns as sound.   

We wanted to meet every requirement of the challenge while building something genuinely useful for both working astronomers and students of any age. Because SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors every six months, making that huge dataset fast, visual, and easy to explore helps anyone interested in infrared astronomy!
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

We built SPHEREx Blink, a browser-based sky explorer that turns real observations from NASA's SPHEREx infrared space telescope into an interactive time-lapse and spectrum viewer. Because SPHEREx captures near-infrared light (0.75 to 5.0 µm across 102 wavelengths) that is completely invisible to the human eye, we translated those hidden colors into images, animations, and sound anyone can explore without installing software.

- formatted with Gemini for enhanced readability from our Github repo documentation.

On the public website, the app streams SPHEREx maps and exposure cutouts straight from NASA's public Amazon S3 bucket, while an optional local Python server adds live multi-archive queries. Type in any star name or sky coordinates to use four main views:

  • Blink: Flip between SPHEREx visits plus 2010 WISE and 2014–2024 NEOWISE photos—just like astronomers once used glass photo plates to discover Pluto—turning slow star movement into a 16-year time-lapse.
  • Difference: Subtract an older visit from a newer one using wavelength-matched images so steady stars cancel out, moving stars show up as amber/cyan pairs, and variable stars brighten or dim.
  • Colour: Mix any of the 102 infrared wavelengths into false-color images, or use presets like methane and water that make cool brown dwarfs glow bright pink.
  • Spectra & Light Curves: Click any star to see its brightness across wavelengths and over time, compare it against Gaia DR3, 2MASS, and AllWISE catalogs, fit temperature curves, or export FITS/CSV files and looping GIFs.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

  • No barriers to real NASA data: Normally, opening SPHEREx's 102-channel FITS files takes specialized desktop tools and custom Python code. We made it work in seconds inside a regular web browser.
  • Built for both astronomers and students: Nothing in the app is simulated. Our brightness and motion measurements are checked against 2MASS, AllWISE, and Gaia DR3 and match within 1 to 3 percent, making it useful for quick research checks while staying clear and fun for students of any age.
  • Export data in multiple research-ready formats: including science-grade FITS files with complete WCS and observation metadata, spectral and light-curve tables (CSV/ECSV), and direct IVOA SAMP integration with tools like TOPCAT and Aladin. Generate publication-quality outputs such as animated comparison GIFs, annotated sky and spectrum figures, multi-color composite PNGs, and shareable links that reproduce the exact view, coordinates, and display settings for collaborators.
  • Intended impact: Because SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors every six months, making that huge dataset fast, visual, and audible helps more people spot moving neighbors, pulsing stars, and chemical fingerprints like water and methane.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Vite, Bun, WebGL2, HTML5 Canvas, Web Audio API, Lucide React, and Aladin Lite v3.
  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.12, uv, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, HTTPX, and pytest.
  • Data & Space Services: NASA SPHEREx Open Data (AWS S3), NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA/TAP, AllWISE, NEOWISE-R, 2MASS), ESA Gaia DR3, CDS Strasbourg (Sesame, VizieR TAP, Aladin Lite), and IVOA SAMP.
  • Hosting & Development: GitHub Pages & GitHub Actions on a Windows 11 PC. All code in the repository is AI-generated using Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

How is it creative and what factors did we consider?

  • Creativity: We combined classic 1930s "blinking" with modern 102-color infrared data across a 16-year multi-mission timeline, and added Web Audio sonification so you can literally hear chemical absorption dips and pulsing stars as sound.
  • We think it's important everyone has access to data in formats that meet them where they are, all while not compromising on professional level quality and tooling. We are really looking forward to feedback so we can see if we hit our goal!
    • Accurate data: No simulated data. We flag saturated star centers (switching to ring measurements when needed) and match wavelengths before subtracting photos so a star's color cannot fake a brightness change. We spent a good chunk of time making sure our processing didn't introduce any data corruption.
    • Speed & reliability: The browser reads only the needed byte ranges from NASA's S3 files, lazy-loads heavy charts, and checks live archive health with smooth fallbacks when external servers go down.
    • Accessibility: Blinking is capped at a safe 3 flashes per second, every chart has plain-English summaries and audio playback, views save directly into shareable URLs, and a guided tour walks first-time visitors through the sky.
